title: Given a string, return the length of the longest subsequence that reads the same forwards and backwards (characters need not be contiguous).

s1_definition.profdef: Interval DP where dp[i][j] is the longest palindromic subsequence length within the substring from i to j. If the ends match, dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j−1]+2; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Equivalent to the LCS of the string with its reverse. Time O(n²), space O(n²).
s1_definition.analogy: A pattern analyst at National Bank of India wants the longest mirror-symmetric pattern inside a code where she may skip characters. If the two ends of a window are the same symbol, they wrap a smaller mirror and add two; if not, she drops whichever end helps more.
s1_definition.oneliner: Ends match ⇒ inner+2; else max of dropping either end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Interval DP where dp[i][j] is the longest palindromic subsequence length within the substring from i to j. If the ends match, dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j−1]+2; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Equivalent to the LCS of the string with its reverse. Time O(n²), space O(n²).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A pattern analyst at National Bank of India wants the longest mirror-symmetric pattern inside a code where she may skip characters. If the two ends of a window are the same symbol, they wrap a smaller mirror and add two; if not, she drops whichever end helps more.

**One line to remember:** Ends match ⇒ inner+2; else max of dropping either end.

sections.s2_technical:
Use a table dp[i][j] over intervals, filled by increasing interval length. Every single character is a palindrome of length one, so dp[i][i] = 1 is the base case. For a window from i to j, if the end characters are equal they contribute two around the best inner palindrome, so dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j−1]+2. For example: `if (s.charAt(i)==s.charAt(j)) dp[i][j]=dp[i+1][j-1]+2;`.

If the ends differ, drop one end and take the better of the two shorter windows: `else dp[i][j]=Math.max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]);`. Because dp[i][j] depends on smaller intervals, iterate i from the end backward and j forward, or iterate by length. The answer is dp[0][n−1].

The time and space are O(n²). A senior nuance is that this exactly equals the longest common subsequence of the string with its reverse, which is a clean alternative derivation, and the subsequence version is harder than the substring version because non-contiguity forbids the simple center expansion.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a pattern analyst searches codes for the longest mirror-symmetric pattern while allowing skipped characters, to detect deliberately embedded symmetric markers. This is exactly how Longest Palindromic Subsequence works.

Problem 2 — Because characters may be skipped, center expansion does not apply and an interval DP is required. This is exactly why dp over substrings by growing length is used.

The mini-project builds a `SymmetryAnalyzer`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input string is bbbab.

Step 1: Every single character cell starts at one as the base case.

Step 2: Adjacent equal pairs like the two b characters give length two by wrapping an empty inner window and adding two.

Step 3: Larger windows with matching ends add two to their inner best, so stretches of b characters accumulate.

Step 4: The full window from index zero to four has ends b and b that match, adding two around the inner best.

Step 5: The answer for the whole string is four, the subsequence bbbb, and cbbd gives two for bb.

```text
2026-10-27T03:30:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Symmetry Analyzer (Palindromic Subsequence)
2026-10-27T03:30:00Z [INFO] Longest palindromic subsequence = 4
2026-10-27T03:30:00Z [INFO] bbbab → 4
2026-10-27T03:30:00Z [INFO] Longest palindromic subsequence = 2
2026-10-27T03:30:00Z [INFO] cbbd → 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  s = b b b a b   (interval DP by growing length)
  dp[i][i]=1
  ends equal ⇒ dp[i][j]=dp[i+1][j-1]+2
  ends differ ⇒ dp[i][j]=max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1])
  dp[0][4] = 4  (subsequence "bbbb")  ≡ LCS(s, reverse(s))
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Palindromic Subsequence is an interval dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the length of the longest palindromic subsequence inside the substring from index i to index j. The base case is that every single character is a palindrome of length one, and I fill the table by growing interval length so that smaller intervals are ready before larger ones.

The transition has two cases. If the two end characters of the window are equal, they wrap around the best inner palindrome and add two to it. If they differ, I drop one end and take the better of the two shorter windows, which is the maximum of excluding the left end or the right end. The answer is the cell covering the whole string.

In my project at National Bank of India, a pattern analyst searched codes for the longest mirror-symmetric pattern while allowing skipped characters, to detect deliberately embedded symmetric markers. Because characters may be skipped, the simple center-expansion trick does not apply, so I used this interval DP, and I like to point out that it is exactly the longest common subsequence of the string with its own reverse.
